tldr: Przybyl explains how Lucene and Elasticsearch use the incubating Panama Vector API for dot products and BBQ quantization, and why Elasticsearch now goes further with a native C++ SIMD kernel called through FFM.
summary: Przybyl starts from the hottest loop in vector search: the dot product over hundreds or thousands of embedding dimensions (Lucene and Elasticsearch support up to 4,096), repeated millions of times per query. SIMD fits that shape: one instruction applied to several primitive values packed into a register, with the number of lanes set by register width (128 bits on his Apple M3 with Neon, 256 or 512 bits with AVX2 or AVX-512 on x86). Lanes are not threads, he stresses, and SIMD does not multiply with core count. His first demo showed a 6-10x Vector API speed-up over a naive loop, until he compared it against a scalar loop that also used four accumulators for instruction-level parallelism and the gain roughly halved. His point: benchmarks lie unless you compare like with like.

He walks through the Vector API vocabulary (VectorSpecies as type plus shape, lanes, fma, reduceLanes), Lucene's dot product with four accumulators and a scalar tail for the remainder, and how C2 turns it into native SIMD instructions. Workloads with branching or avalanche-style hashing, such as Elasticsearch's routing hash for auto-generated document IDs, are poor fits. Lucene enables the Vector API only on HotSpot with C2, when jdk.incubator.vector is added as a module and when the preferred vector size is at least 128 bits; otherwise it falls back to scalar code silently. He showed the 'Java vector incubator API enabled, preferred bit size 128' log line from a local Elasticsearch.

The main case study is Better Binary Quantization (BBQ): documents are stored at 1 bit per dimension using a centroid rather than a zero threshold, while queries use 4 bits (asymmetric encoding). Query nibbles are rearranged into bit planes so scoring becomes bitwise AND, popcount and shifts, with no multiplication. One million 768-dimension vectors shrink from about 3 GB to about 100 MB, and a two-phase search oversamples candidates and rescores them. He used PrintAssembly with hsdis to confirm Neon and YMM registers were actually in use.

Przybyl said that from Elasticsearch 9.5 the vector search path no longer relies on the Vector API on supported Linux machines: a C++ library (simdvec) with per-architecture kernels ships as .so files inside the JAR and is called through the Foreign Function and Memory API on JDK 22+ heap segments, falling back to the Vector API and then to scalar code. The reason is that the Java abstraction still leaks: fma is slower than mul plus add on Apple Silicon, and Lucene has a heuristic for exactly that. The Vector API is still used elsewhere, for example for SIMD probing of Swiss-style hash tables in ES|QL bucketing.
keyPoints: A naive Vector API dot product looked 6-10x faster than scalar code, but against a scalar loop with four accumulators (instruction-level parallelism) the gain was roughly half that.

Lucene only activates its Panama implementation on HotSpot with C2, with the jdk.incubator.vector module added and a preferred vector size of at least 128 bits; otherwise it uses a scalar fallback without any user action.
SIMD suits simple arithmetic over large primitive arrays; branchy code and avalanche-style hashing such as document ID routing are poor fits, and SIMD gains do not multiply with core count.
BBQ stores document vectors at 1 bit per dimension (centroid-based) and queries at 4 bits, scoring with AND, popcount and shifts; 1 million 768-dimension vectors go from about 3 GB to about 100 MB.
Use -XX:+PrintAssembly with hsdis to verify that intended vectorization, not long-standing auto-vectorization, produced the SIMD instructions (Neon registers on ARM, YMM with AVX2).

fma versus mul followed by add performs differently per CPU: mul plus add is faster on Apple Silicon and they are on par on his Intel machine, so Lucene includes an Apple Silicon heuristic and a flag to override it.
According to Przybyl, Elasticsearch 9.5 calls a bundled native C++ SIMD kernel through FFM first, then falls back to the Vector API, then to scalar code; the native path does not run on Windows.
ES|QL uses SIMD probing of a cache-friendly Swiss-table structure to speed up hash lookups when bucketing large time ranges.
takeaways: Benchmark Vector API code against a scalar baseline that uses the same accumulator and ILP tricks before claiming a speed-up.
Run with --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector and check Elasticsearch or Lucene logs to confirm the vectorized path is active on your hardware.
Check JIT output with PrintAssembly and hsdis on the actual production CPU type, since ARM and x86 behave differently.
Try BBQ or other quantization tiers for large vector indexes when RAM and disk, not recall, are the constraint.
Keep a scalar fallback and runtime capability checks whenever you adopt an incubating API in production code.

quotes.text: There are lies, damn lies, and there are benchmarks.
Even if you're reaching the limits of Java, Java allows you to then go beyond it in C++.

watchIf: You write numeric hot loops in Java, run Elasticsearch vector search, or want to know whether the incubating Vector API is ready for production use.
